subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage: In the Saturday sign class at the community centre, Tanuja held her hand flat near her chest, palm facing herself. "Now watch," said their teacher, and turned the palm outward, the same shape, the same movement. "Same hand. Different word." Nikita blinked. She'd assumed signs were like waving, loose and free, so who would care about the palm? "It's like vowels," the teacher signed and said aloud. "Change 'cat' to 'cot' and it's another word." Nikita practised in front of the window, palm in, palm out, carefully. When she got it wrong, the teacher gently corrected her hand. Nikita thought, this is a real language, with grammar, and I have to respect it. Tanuja gave her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: Where did the sign class meet?
qa.a: The sign class met at the community centre.

qa.q: Why did Nikita blink when the teacher turned the palm outward?
qa.a: She was surprised because she had assumed signs were loose gestures where palm direction would not matter. She then understood it changes the word.

qa.q: What could Nikita do to learn signs properly?
qa.a: Practise palm direction and handshape carefully and accept corrections, treating signing as a language with rules.

qa.q: How might a deaf signer feel if a hearing learner treated signs as loose gestures?
qa.a: They might feel disrespected, because their language has grammar and precision.

grounding: Palm direction changes a sign's meaning like a vowel changes a word, and hearing learners must respect that grammar.

"Watch my hand," said Gargi. "Palm toward me, then palm away. Same shape, different meaning."
"They look the same to me," said Harsha, squinting.
"How the palm faces and how the hand is aimed are part of the word, like a vowel. Change it, and it means something else."
"So I can't just wave my hand around?"
"Not if you want to be understood. Try again. Slowly."
Harsha tried, palm in, then out. Gargi signed, 'Yes, that one,' and laughed. "It's a proper language, not gestures. My cousin says people get this wrong all the time."
"Then I'd better get it right," said Harsha.

qa.q: What does Gargi say is part of the word?
qa.a: Gargi says how the palm faces and how the hand is aimed are part of the word.

qa.q: Why did Harsha squint and ask about just waving a hand around?
qa.a: Harsha believed signs were loose gestures and struggled to see the difference. The question shows Harsha had not yet understood the grammar.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to improve?
qa.a: Practise slowly with palm direction, accept Gargi's feedback and treat signing as a real language.

qa.q: How might Gargi's cousin feel when people treat signs as gestures?
qa.a: They may feel frustrated or disrespected, because their language is being ignored. 🙂

grounding: Palm direction and hand orientation carry meaning in signed languages, like vowels.

subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage:
When I started learning Indian Sign Language with Chaitanya, who is Deaf and sits next to me in art, I thought signs were like gestures. Roughly right was good enough.
Then one lunch I signed a sentence with my palm facing out instead of facing me. Chaitanya's face went blank, then he laughed and shook his head. He showed me both versions, side by side. Same hand shape. Different direction. Completely different meaning.
"Like a vowel," he wrote on my notebook. "Bat. Bit. Not the same word."
That changed how I saw it. I'd been treating his language like loose waving. It has rules as exact as English spelling.
Now I practise with a mirror, checking where my palm points. I still get it wrong. But when I do, I ask Chaitanya to show me again, and he does.
- Elizabeth

qa.q: What did Chaitanya write on Elizabeth's notebook?
qa.a: "Like a vowel. Bat. Bit. Not the same word."

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Chaitanya's face went blank?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt embarrassed and confused, realising the sign hadn't meant what was intended.

qa.q: What small step helps Elizabeth improve now?
qa.a: Practising with a mirror to check palm direction and asking Chaitanya to show the sign again when unsure.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have seen Elizabeth's early signing?
qa.a: He probably saw it as well-meant but careless, as if his language were loose gestures rather than a language with exact rules.

grounding: The account shows a hearing learner discovering that palm direction changes a sign's meaning and respecting it as grammar.

subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage:
Teacher's note - Gurleen, Sign language club, Wednesday
Damini is one of our most enthusiastic hearing learners. She has a large vocabulary for three months. But today, during the story round, the Deaf students kept looking puzzled at her.
When I watched closely, the problem was her palms. She'd get the hand shape right but let her hand face any direction. In this language, direction can change the word itself.
I asked her to sign two signs that differ only in where the palm faces. She did them the same way. When I showed her the difference, she looked surprised, then a bit embarrassed.
I told her it is like pronouncing a vowel wrongly in English, not a small detail.
She spent the rest of the session practising slowly with a partner, checking her palm every time. She said, "I thought I was being lazy. Actually I didn't know it mattered."

qa.q: How long had Damini been learning?
qa.a: For three months.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when Gurleen showed her the difference?
qa.a: Damini was surprised and a bit embarrassed, realising that the direction of her palms had been changing her words.

qa.q: How did Gurleen help Damini understand the problem?
qa.a: She had Damini sign two signs that differed only in palm direction, then compared it to mispronouncing a vowel in English.

qa.q: How might the Deaf students have experienced Damini's story?
qa.a: They were probably confused, seeing signs that looked almost right but meant something else because of the palm direction.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a hearing learner learning that palm direction is part of a sign's grammar, not a loose detail.

passage:
Saturday
Sign practice at the community centre with Keerthana today. She's Deaf and is the most patient teacher on earth.
I've been learning for two months and I thought I was doing well. Then I signed something about my weekend, and Keerthana stopped me and laughed. Not meanly. She showed me: I'd had my palm facing down when it should face up. Same shape, same movement. Different meaning.
I went hot in the face. I'd been doing it wrong for weeks!
But she wrote on her phone: "Everyone does this. Hearing people think hands are for waving. Hands are grammar."
Hands are grammar. I keep thinking about that.
We practised the palm-up and palm-down pair ten times. She made me look at her face too, because apparently that's part of it.
Next week I'm going to film myself and check.
- Indu

qa.q: How long has Indu been learning?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when Keerthana pointed out the mistake?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed, going hot in the face, but also grateful because Keerthana laughed kindly, not meanly.

qa.q: What will Indu try next week, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Filming the signing to check palm direction, because small changes in orientation can change a sign's meaning.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see hearing learners' mistakes?
qa.a: Keerthana seems patient and understanding, seeing them as common, while still insisting the grammar matters.

grounding: The diary shows a hearing learner discovering that palm orientation changes a sign's meaning and treating signs as grammar, not gestures.
